To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) when recalling familiar routes, participants generated more details in a detail condition that encouraged episodic retrieval and (2) when using the recalled route to solve navigation problems, participants in the detail condition were more likely to generate spatial references and to use the familiar route as a basis for their solutions.

a detailed approach to remembering routes led to more detailed descriptions of routes, more accurate route recall, and better learning of a new spatial environment, whereas a gist approach to remembering routes produced more spatial references, less accurate route recall, but better learning of the spatial environment.
the many routes of mental navigational retrieval have different effects on how familiar route information can be used and how new routes can be encoded.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of episodic memory processes in spatial cognition.
how spatial representations can be flexibly retrieved and used and how they can be formed in novel spatial environments.
the role of episodic memory for spatial cognition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the gist condition is more effective in retrieving spatial information from memory, while the detail condition promotes the flexible use and formation of spatial representations.

the many routes of mental spatial navigation can be recalled by using different remembering approaches that engage different processes and have different consequences for how familiar and novel routes can be recalled and flexibly used.

the gist condition led to the use of a schematic representation of familiar routes, while in the detail condition a more episodic representation of the familiar route was used, which in turn led to a higher level of spatial flexibility.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the many ways to remember routes can have distinct effects on how we use familiar spatial information and on how we form new spatial representations.
episodic processes at recall are important for flexibly navigating in a familiar environment and for forming spatial representations of novel environments.
a schematic retrieval approach can be useful for navigating around familiar routes but may be detrimental when learning new spatial representations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
different remembering approaches can have different effects on how spatial representations can be retrieved, flexibly used, and formed.
the way in which we remember familiar information influences how we use this information to solve problems and to learn new information.
the retrieval approach can be a powerful tool in studying how people use and form spatial representations.
